The purpose of this post is to share some stuff with you that I did a while back. It's an analytical approach to staying anonymous online.

Any time I create an online handle or profile, I decide what types of anonymity I need associated with that handle for the type of content I will be posting under that handle.

Mostly Forward Anonymous

Can any random Internet person, using only my handle, figure out my real name, using only information from my profile and public databases?

This is what people usually worry about when they try to keep an online account anonymous. But it's not the only type of anonymity to keep in mind.

Perfectly Forward Anonymous

Can people with connections to the content shared in this profile identify me?

If you use your profile to tell true stories from your real life, you're at risk here. If the story gets seen by a large enough audience (worst case - goes viral), there's a chance it will be seen by characters from your story. If those people can identify you from your profile, you're not perfectly forward anonymous.

People most often blow perfect forward anonymity by telling stories about customers from their work.

If you want to tell true stories from your real life, it's best to fudge some of the details about the timeline and characters so they don't recognize it's the same story. (Or even if they do - and come barging into your work shoving a copy of the story in your manager's face, the manager will be like "umm sorry honey this isn't my store.")

Reverse Anonymous

Can a person I know in real life figure out my Internet handle?

Pretty self explanatory. If you leave your account signed in with the alias in plain view of coworkers, family, friends, enemies, etc, then you're not reverse anonymous. Another way to blow it would be talking about posts you submitted, or arguments you had, with the people in your real life. You're giving them the power to figure out your online alias and dox you.

Legally Anonymous

Can a person with only the information publicly available in my profile, and the full power of government, identify me?

There's lots of online information available about this one. The only way to stay legally anonymous is to use an anonymizing proxy like Tor (or surf from public hotspots, preferably without video surveillance), and properly configure your workstation's privacy settings. If your only goal is to trigger tumblrinas and post politically incorrect content, you probably don't need legal anonymity.

Testably Anonymous

Can a person who thinks they've connected your online alias to your identity establish reasonably well that they got it right?

This is probaby the most important one of all these, because it's your second level of security. If a crazy sjw thinks they might have an idea who you are, or have narrowed your identity down to one of a few candidates, will the information in your profile support their claim?

For example: assume Jill has posted, over several weeks, that she has a 4 year old nephew, recently travelled to Italy, and works in a 5-story office building. She also recently provided tech support to a person in removing malware from their PC, exposing that she has a technical background.

Now a batshit insane sjw tries to dox Jill. None of those details are easy to search on, so they wouldn't help the sjw find Jill in a crowd the size of the Internet. But if the sjw narrows the search down some other way, or perhaps knows Jill in real life and thinks this online alias might be hers, then these details would be enough to remove all doubt.

Jill could have protected herself by not posting those details, fudging them slightly (6 year old nephew?), or posting other details that were false. If the online alias claimed to be 5 years older with a masters degree in a field Jill knows nothing about, then the sjw might conclude it wasn't actually Jill.

Adding an example of how a perfectly forward anonymous, but not testably anonymous, account could get doxed by a random SJW:

Let's say Jill has done a good job with perfect forward anonymity, but has a habit of frequently posting videos from a low-subscriber youtube channel shortly after the videos go up.

An SJW might conclude that Jill probably subscribes to that channel. Even though the SJW can't see the subscribers list, she can look at people who frequently comment on the channel. From that, the SJW might have identified a dozen or so youtube accounts that might be Jills.

The SJW would then go through the list one at a time, researching and excluding each candidate individually. If Jill had a Testably Anonymous account, she would get excluded. But if there was a high degree of overlap between details from Jill's youtube account and anonymous online alias, Jill would get doxxed.
